title: Milestone: Colonies to a House Divided
objective: After this level you can connect colonial slavery, the founders' compromises and westward expansion to explain why the nation split by 1860.
summary: Lincoln’s 1858 House Divided speech names where the first half of the story led: a nation half slave and half free. Tobacco, slave laws, compromises, cotton and new land all fed the split.

cards.headline: Milestone: halfway through US history. Why was the nation coming apart?
cards.body: From Jamestown’s tobacco to Bleeding Kansas, the first half of this story kept circling one question: where would slavery stand? Put it all together.

cards.headline: A house divided
cards.body: On June 16, 1858, in Springfield, Illinois, Abraham Lincoln put the chapter’s problem in one sentence: "A house divided against itself cannot stand." He added: "I believe this government cannot endure, permanently half slave and half free." Cotton had made slavery more profitable, and each new territory reopened the question the compromises had tried to settle.

cards.headline: The road to a house divided

events.label: The Liberator appears; Nat Turner’s revolt
Seneca Falls; Mexico cedes about 55 percent of its land

cards.headline: Milestone: a house divided
learned: How Native nations lived before 1492, and how disease, Spain and English tobacco colonies changed North America.
How colonial laws turned slavery into a lifelong, inherited status, even as colonists learned to govern themselves.
Why the Revolution’s language of liberty moved the North to begin ending slavery, and who it still left out.
What the Constitution’s compromises over slavery settled in 1787, and what they left for later.
Why cotton, new land and failed compromises left the nation half slave and half free by 1858.

questions.prompt: Why did Jamestown’s tobacco boom lead to war with the Powhatan in 1622?

options.label: The Powhatan wanted to control the tobacco trade
options.rationale: The trouble was land: tobacco led settlers to press onto Native land.

options.label: Growing it pushed settlers onto more Powhatan land
Pocahontas’s marriage to Rolfe had broken the peace
options.rationale: The 1614 marriage brought peace, for a time.

options.label: England banned tobacco, so the colony turned to raiding
options.rationale: Rolfe’s tobacco sold well in England.

questions.explanation: Tobacco paid, so settlers pressed further into Native land. In 1622 Opechancanough’s warriors struck back.

questions.prompt: How did colonial law make slavery a status passed down through generations?

options.label: The Constitution of 1787 said so in plain words
options.rationale: The Constitution never used the word slavery, and this came over a century earlier.

options.label: Every colony copied Spain’s laws from St. Augustine
options.rationale: English colonies wrote their own laws, court by court.

options.label: Virginia’s 1662 law tied a child’s status to the father’s
options.rationale: That was the English rule Virginia reversed.

options.label: Virginia’s 1662 law tied a child’s status to the mother’s

questions.explanation: In 1662 Virginia made a child enslaved or free according to the mother, reversing the English rule, so slavery passed from mother to child.

questions.prompt: After the Revolution, how did slavery begin to end in the North?

options.label: Through freedom suits and gradual abolition laws
Through a clause in the Declaration of Independence
options.rationale: The Declaration freed no one; Congress even cut Jefferson’s slave-trade passage.

options.label: Through a single act of Congress freeing everyone
options.rationale: It happened state by state, from 1780 to 1804.

options.label: Through Lord Dunmore’s offer to Loyalists’ enslaved people
options.rationale: Dunmore’s offer was aimed at rebels’ enslaved people, not Loyalists’.

questions.explanation: Elizabeth Freeman won her freedom in court in 1781, and Pennsylvania’s 1780 law began gradual abolition. Other northern states followed by 1804, while the South kept slavery.

questions.prompt: When the Constitution of 1787 divided House seats among the states, how were enslaved people counted?

options.label: They were left out entirely, since they could not vote
options.rationale: They were counted, as “all other Persons.”

options.label: Each one counted fully, the same as a free person
options.rationale: The clause counted three-fifths, not all.

options.label: Three-fifths of them counted, though never named
Only in states that had banned the slave trade
options.rationale: The count applied in every state that held enslaved people.

questions.explanation: The three-fifths clause counted enslaved people as “all other Persons” for House seats and direct taxes, without ever using the word slave.

questions.prompt: The Louisiana Purchase of 1803 doubled the country. How did it lead to the Missouri Compromise of 1820?

options.label: It made Missouri the first free state west of the Mississippi
options.rationale: Missouri entered as a slave state.

options.label: Missouri, carved from it, asked to join as a slave state
It ended the argument by opening all of it to slavery
options.rationale: The compromise banned slavery north of 36°30′ in the rest of it.

options.label: Native nations sold the land directly to Missouri’s settlers
options.rationale: The purchase bought only France’s claim to the land.

questions.explanation: Admitting Missouri as a slave state upset the balance, so Congress added free Maine and a line at 36°30′ across the rest of the Louisiana Territory.

questions.prompt: Eli Whitney’s gin saved labor. So why did the number of people forced to grow cotton keep rising?

options.label: Each machine needed several enslaved workers to turn it
options.rationale: The gin itself saved labor; demand grew in the fields.

options.label: Congress required planters to use one on every farm
options.rationale: No law did this; profit did.

options.label: It worked only on coastal long-staple cotton
options.rationale: It made sticky-seeded inland cotton worth growing.

options.label: It sped up only cleaning, and profits drove planters to expand

questions.explanation: Planting, hoeing and picking still took people. Cotton grew so profitable that enslavers demanded more land and more enslaved workers.

questions.prompt: Put these events on the road to a house divided in order, from earliest to latest.
questions.explanation: The Indian Removal Act passed in 1830, Nat Turner’s revolt came in 1831, Seneca Falls in 1848, the Kansas-Nebraska Act in 1854, and Lincoln’s House Divided speech in 1858.
